anchorCharts.name: Author's Purpose
anchorCharts.body: Authors write to persuade, inform, entertain, or explain. Look for clues: facts often inform, directions explain, strong opinions persuade, and story events entertain.
ex: A tall tale about an amazing firefighter is mostly written to entertain.
An article that gives facts about food groups is mostly written to inform.
A poster asking families to use reusable containers is written to persuade.

anchorCharts.name: Intended Audience
anchorCharts.body: The intended audience is who the author is writing for. Clues include the title, word choice, pictures, examples, and what the author asks readers to do.
ex: A school lunch poster with simple labels may be for students and families.
A recipe with step-by-step directions may be for cooks or people preparing food.
A safety notice with rules may be for people who visit a place.

anchorCharts.name: Ideas and Support
anchorCharts.body: An idea is what the author wants readers to understand. Supporting details are facts, examples, reasons, or story events that prove or explain the idea.
ex: Idea: A balanced lunch gives students energy. Support: Whole grains, protein, fruits, vegetables, and water help the body work.
Idea: A character is brave. Support: She helps others even when the job is difficult.

anchorCharts.name: Figurative Language
anchorCharts.body: Figurative language makes writing vivid. A simile compares two things using like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another. Hyperbole is a huge exaggeration.
ex: "His shovel was as big as a train car" is a simile.
"The city was an oven" is a metaphor.
"I have told you a million times" is hyperbole.

anchorCharts.name: Central Idea
anchorCharts.body: The central idea is the most important point of a nonfiction text or section. It is bigger than one detail and should be a complete sentence.
ex: Topic: insect hotels. Central idea: Insect hotels can give helpful insects a safe place to rest and lay eggs.
Topic: healthy cooking. Central idea: Small choices in the kitchen can help families build healthier meals.

anchorCharts.name: Text and Graphic Features
anchorCharts.body: Headings, captions, labels, charts, diagrams, sidebars, and bold words help readers find and understand information.
ex: A chart can compare two choices quickly.
Labels on a diagram can name important parts.
A sidebar can give extra facts without interrupting the main text.

passages.title: Penny Pepper and the Giant Soup Pot
passages.body:
This story is a tall tale. A tall tale is a story with unbelievable and fantastic details, told as if it were true and factual.

1 Penny Pepper lived in a windy town called Spoonville. She was nothing like the other cooks. People said she could stir soup with one hand and lift a flour sack with one finger. Her laugh was as loud as a school bell, so everyone knew when Penny was in the kitchen.

2 One winter morning, a snowstorm covered Spoonville. The roads disappeared under drifts of snow, and the town's food delivery wagon could not get through. Families were hungry, and the mayor worried that there would not be enough lunch for the school.

3 Penny looked at the empty pantry and then at the frozen pond. She got an idea. She rolled her biggest soup pot to the pond and chopped a circle in the ice. Then she pulled carrots from her garden, shook snow from a mountain of potatoes, and added one onion that made the whole town cry.

4 Penny stirred and stirred until steam rose higher than the clock tower. The smell floated down every street. Children carried bowls, parents brought spoons, and even the mayor brought a loaf of bread. Within an hour, every person in Spoonville had warm soup.

5 By sunset, the storm had stopped. The next spring, the place where Penny chopped the ice became the town's first public well. People still say Penny's soup was so hot it melted winter itself.

questions.sampleAnswer: Penny was different because she was extremely strong, had a very loud laugh, and could make enough soup to feed the whole town.

passages.title: The Lunch Tray Team
passages.body:
A healthy lunch does not need to be fancy. It needs balance. A balanced meal gives your body energy, helps your brain stay alert, and keeps you from feeling hungry too soon.

[Chart: A balanced tray can include 1 fruit, 1 vegetable, 1 grain, 1 protein, and water or milk.]

At West Park School, a group of fourth graders called themselves the Lunch Tray Team. They noticed that many students ate only chips or sweets at lunch. The team made a poster for the cafeteria. It showed a tray with labeled sections for apple slices, carrots, brown rice, chicken, and water.

The poster did not tell students to stop eating treats forever. Instead, it asked them to add one healthy choice each day. On Monday, students could add fruit. On Tuesday, they could try a vegetable. By Friday, many students were building meals with more colors and fewer empty calories.

The principal liked the poster because it was clear and friendly. Younger students could understand the labels, and families saw the same idea in the weekly school newsletter.

choices: A balanced lunch can help students have energy and make healthier choices.

Only fourth graders need vegetables.

choices: It showed a tray with labeled sections.

It had no pictures.

choices: The parts of a balanced tray
The price of school lunch
The names of every fourth grader
The history of West Park School

choices: Younger students in the cafeteria

Only bus drivers

choices: Add one healthy choice each day

choices: To show a simple sequence students could follow

questions.sampleAnswer: One detail is that the poster asked students to add one healthy choice each day instead of changing everything at once.

passages.title: Bug Hotel Helpers
passages.body:
Not every bug in a garden is a pest. Bees, ladybugs, and lacewings can help plants grow or protect them from harmful insects. One way to welcome helpful insects is to build a small bug hotel.

A bug hotel is a box filled with natural materials. Hollow stems give tiny bees a safe place to lay eggs. Pinecones and dry leaves make hiding spots for ladybugs. Small sticks create cracks where insects can rest away from wind and rain.

[Diagram: A bug hotel has sections labeled hollow stems, pinecones, dry leaves, and sticks.]

A school garden club made signs beside its bug hotel. The signs reminded visitors not to shake the box or spray chemicals nearby. The club wrote the signs for students, families, and anyone who walked through the garden.

After a month, the garden had more flowers and fewer aphids. The club could not see every insect at work, but the plants looked healthier. Sometimes the smallest helpers make a big difference.

choices: After a month, the garden had more flowers and fewer aphids.

choices: True

questions.sampleAnswer: A bug hotel can be useful because it gives helpful insects safe places to rest or lay eggs, and those insects can help plants grow or protect them from pests.

passages.title: Rocks Tell Stories
passages.body:
Rocks may look silent, but they can tell stories about Earth. A smooth pebble may show that water rolled it for a long time. A rock with tiny shell marks may tell scientists that the place was once under the sea.

There are three main kinds of rocks. Igneous rocks form when melted rock cools. Sedimentary rocks form when layers of sand, mud, or shells press together. Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change one kind of rock into another.

[Sidebar: The word metamorphic comes from words that mean changed form.]

A geologist studies rocks like a detective studies clues. The color, shape, layers, and fossils all matter. A dark, glassy rock might come from a volcano. A striped rock might show years of pressure deep underground.

The next time you pick up a stone, do not think of it as ordinary. It may be a tiny page from Earth's very old book.

"Igneous rocks form when melted rock cools."

choices: To inform readers about how rocks can show clues about Earth
To persuade readers to stop collecting rocks
To entertain readers with a tall tale about a giant rock

choices: A smooth pebble may show that water rolled it for a long time.

choices: Layers of sand, mud, or shells press together.

questions.sampleAnswer: A geologist might study a rock's color, shape, layers, fossils, shell marks, or whether it is dark and glassy.

passages.title: Why Your Body Loves Sleep
passages.body:
Have you ever wondered why you spend almost a third of your life with your eyes closed? Sleep may look like doing nothing, but inside your body it is one of the busiest times of the entire day.

1 While you sleep, your brain works like a librarian after closing time. During the day, you collect thousands of new facts, sounds, and feelings. At night, your brain sorts through that enormous pile, files away what matters, and quietly clears out what does not. Scientists believe this is one reason students who sleep well often remember their lessons more easily than students who stay up late.

2 Your body repairs itself at night, too. Tiny tears in your muscles heal, your bones grow stronger, and your immune system builds defenders to fight off germs. This is why a person who is getting sick is so often told to rest. Sleep is not a reward you earn after a hard day; it is part of the hard work itself.

[Chart: Recommended sleep each night — Ages 6 to 12: 9 to 12 hours. Ages 13 to 18: 8 to 10 hours.]

3 So what happens when we skip it? A tired brain is like a phone with a dying battery. It still switches on, but it runs slowly, drops things, and grows cranky. Researchers have found that students who do not get enough sleep struggle more to pay attention, solve problems, and control their feelings. Missing sleep does not just make you yawn. It changes how well your whole brain can work the next day.

4 The good news is that better sleep is a habit almost anyone can build. Going to bed at the same time each night trains your body to feel sleepy on schedule. Dimming bright screens an hour before bed helps as well, because the blue light from phones and tablets can trick your brain into thinking it is still daytime. A cool, dark, quiet room sends one clear message to your body: it is finally time to rest.

5 Sleep is free, it needs no special equipment, and it is one of the most powerful tools you have for staying healthy. So the next time someone tells you to go to bed, remember that you are not wasting a single minute. You are giving your brain and body the night shift they need to keep you strong, sharp, and ready for tomorrow.

questions.sampleAnswer: One habit is dimming bright screens an hour before bed. It works because the blue light from phones and tablets can trick the brain into thinking it is still daytime, which makes it harder to feel sleepy.

passages.title: The Long Journey of a Strawberry
passages.body:
Pick up a fresh strawberry in the middle of winter and you may be holding a world traveler. The fruit on your plate has sometimes journeyed farther in a single week than many people travel in a whole year.

1 The distance food travels from a farm to your fork is called food miles. A strawberry grown far away might ride on a truck, then a giant ship, then another truck before it finally reaches your store. Every mile burns fuel, and burning fuel releases gases that can slowly warm the planet. A short trip from a nearby farm uses far less fuel than a long voyage across an ocean.

2 This is one reason many families try to eat food that is local and in season. Local food is usually picked when it is ripe, instead of being picked early so it can survive a long trip. Food that is in season is often cheaper as well, because farmers are not fighting the weather to grow it.

[Chart: Average distance food travels — Local farm to table: under 100 miles. Out-of-season imported fruit: often more than 1,500 miles.]

3 Eating, though, is only half of the story. About one third of all the food grown in the world is never eaten at all. It spoils inside trucks, sits forgotten at the back of refrigerators, or gets scraped straight into the trash. When that wasted food rots in a landfill, it releases a gas called methane that traps heat far more powerfully than the exhaust from a car.

4 Many schools have discovered a clever answer hiding right in their lunchrooms: the compost bin. Instead of tossing apple cores and banana peels into the garbage, students drop them into a bin where worms and tiny microbes break them down. Months later, those scraps become dark, rich soil that the school garden uses to grow even more food. The cycle closes like a door clicking quietly shut, with almost nothing wasted.

5 No single child can fix the planet's food problem alone. But choosing a local apple, finishing a packed lunch, or tossing a peel into a compost bin are all small choices that add up. When millions of people make the very same small choice on the same day, the result is anything but small.

choices: The choices we make about where food comes from and how much we waste can help the planet.

choices: The distance food travels from a farm to your fork

questions.sampleAnswer: A student could put apple cores and banana peels into a compost bin instead of the trash, so the scraps turn into rich soil for a garden instead of rotting in a landfill and releasing methane.

passages.title: The Science Hidden in Your Kitchen
passages.body:
A kitchen may be the most interesting science lab you will ever visit. Every single time someone cooks a meal, chemistry, heat, and even a little bit of math quietly go to work.

1 Think about what happens to bread inside a toaster. Cold, pale bread goes in, and warm, golden toast comes out. Heat causes the sugars and proteins in the bread to change and turn brown. Scientists call this the browning reaction, and it is the same process that gives a grilled cheese its crisp edges and a cookie its golden top. Cooking, in other words, is not simply heating food. It is changing it.

2 Cooking can also make food safer and easier for our bodies to use. Heat softens tough vegetables so we can pull more nutrients from them, and it kills germs that might otherwise make us sick. This is one reason humans have cooked their food for thousands of years, long before anyone understood the science hidden behind it.

[Sidebar: A nutrition label lists the serving size, calories, and the amounts of fat, sugar, protein, and vitamins in a food. Comparing two labels can quickly show which choice gives your body more of what it needs.]

3 Smart cooks are also smart readers. The nutrition label on a package is like a report card for food. It tells you how much sugar, salt, fat, and protein a single serving holds. Two boxes of cereal may look almost identical on the front, and yet one may contain twice the sugar of the other. A reader who checks the label can choose the breakfast that gives steady energy instead of a quick rush followed by a crash.

4 You do not need fancy tools to cook well. A sharp knife, a hot pan, and a little patience can turn plain ingredients into a real meal. Measuring carefully matters, too. Baking especially is a kind of edible math, where one small mistake with the flour or the salt can change the entire result.

5 So the next time you stand in a kitchen, look closely. The bubbling pot, the browning toast, and the slowly rising bread are not magic. They are science you can actually taste, and with a few good habits, they are science you can use to take better care of yourself.

choices: A simile comparing a label to a report card
A heading that begins a new section

choices: True

choices: To inform readers that everyday cooking is full of useful science

questions.sampleAnswer: A nutrition label tells you how much sugar, salt, fat, and protein is in a serving. By comparing labels, a person can pick the food with less sugar or more protein, which gives steadier energy instead of a quick rush and a crash.

passages.title: Could Insects Be the Food of the Future?
passages.body:
Imagine a snack that is packed with protein, costs very little to raise, and barely harms the planet. Now imagine that this snack is a cricket. To billions of people around the world, eating insects is nothing strange at all.

1 Eating insects even has its own scientific name: entomophagy. In many countries, fried grasshoppers, roasted ants, and toasted crickets are sold as ordinary food, the same way popcorn or pretzels are sold in other places. Some scientists believe that as the world's population keeps growing, insects could become an important food for everyone.

2 Why are researchers so interested in bugs? The answer is mostly about resources. Raising cattle for beef uses enormous amounts of land, water, and grain. Crickets, by comparison, need very little of any of these. To produce the same amount of protein, crickets use only a tiny fraction of the water that cows do, and they take up far less space.

[Chart: Water needed to make one pound of protein — Beef: about 1,800 gallons. Crickets: about 1 gallon.]

3 Insects are also surprisingly nutritious. Many are rich in protein, healthy fats, iron, and vitamins. Gram for gram, some insects carry nearly as much protein as meat. Because they can be raised in stacked trays indoors, insect farms can grow food in small spaces, even in crowded cities where there is no room for wide fields of cattle.

4 Still, there is one large hurdle, and it is not science. It is feeling. Many people who did not grow up eating insects find the whole idea unpleasant. To get around this, some companies grind insects into a fine powder and bake it into chips, pasta, and energy bars. Hidden inside familiar foods, the protein arrives without the crunch of legs or wings. A bug you cannot see, it turns out, is a bug many people are finally willing to try.

5 No one is saying you must replace every meal with beetles. But the next time you hear someone shriek at the sight of a bug, remember this: that tiny creature might hold a clue to feeding a hungry, crowded planet. The food of the future may already be living in the grass beneath your feet.

choices: To inform readers about edible insects and persuade them to keep an open mind

questions.q: Explain one reason crickets might be a better protein source for the planet than cattle.
questions.sampleAnswer: Crickets need far less water and land than cattle to make the same amount of protein. For example, beef takes about 1,800 gallons of water per pound of protein, while crickets take only about 1 gallon, and crickets can be raised in stacked trays in small spaces.
